{{smaller|'''Breeding in the line''', breeding from animals of the same variety, but of different parentage.='''Syn. 1.''' Generation, production.—'''2.''' Raising.—'''3.''' Training, discipline.}}

'''breeding-cage''' (brē′ding-kāj), ''n.'' '''1.''' A contrivance used by entomologists for rearing insects in captivity, as a box of wire netting, a jar covered with cloth, or any similar arrangement.—'''2.''' A large cage, with a box, pan, or compartment for a nest, in which a pair of birds are placed for breeding in captivity.

'''breeding-pen''' (brē′ding-pen), ''n.'' '''1.''' A pen or inclosure, or a yard with the necessary house for shelter, in which animals or poultry are confined for the purpose of producing pure-bred stock.—'''2.''' At exhibitions of poultry, a certain number of females, commonly four, but sometimes five, shown, together with a male, in competition for a prize.

'''breedling†''' (brēd′ling), ''n.'' [< ''breed'' + ''-ling''<sup>1</sup>.] A native; an inhabitant.
{{smaller block|Over most sad fens, all the way observing the sad life which the people of the place—which, if they be born there, they do call the ''Breedlings'' of the place—do live.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, Sept. 17, 1663.}}}}

'''breek'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' Scotch, northern English, and obsolete form of ''breech''.

'''breek'''<sup>2</sup>'''†''', ''n.'' An obsolete or dialectal variant of ''break'' or ''breach''.

'''breeks''' (brēks), ''n. pl.'' Scotch and northern English form of ''breeches''.

'''breitoline''' (brī′tō-lin), ''n.'' [Named for the inventor, L. ''Breit.''] A musical instrument of the violin family, having five metal strings and a compass somewhat lower than a viola. It is fastened upon a table, like a zither, and played with a bow.

'''breloque''' (bre-lok′), ''n.'' [F.; origin uncertain.] A seal, locket, charm, or other small trinket or article of jewelry attached to a watch-chain.

'''breme†''', ''a.'' See ''brim''<sup>4</sup>.

'''bremely†''', ''adv.'' See ''brimly.''

'''Bremen blue, green,''' etc. See the nouns.

'''bremly†''', ''adv.'' See ''brimly.''

'''bren<sup>1</sup>†''' (bren), ''v.'' [< ME. ''brennen'', the usual form of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.] An obsolete or dialectal variant of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Closely the wicked flame his bowels ''brent.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 16.}}
The Romaines this Night [Candlemas Day] went about the City of Rome, with Torches and Candles ''brenning'' in Worship of this Woman Februa, for hope to have the more Helpe and Succoure of her sonne Mars.
{{right|''J. Brand'', in Bourne’s Pop. Antiq. (1777), p. 224.}}}}

'''bren<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''bran''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''brennage''' (bren′āj), ''n.'' [< OF. ''brenage'' (ML. ''brenagium''), < ''bren'', ML. ''brennium'', bran: see ''bran''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''old law'', a tribute or composition which tenants paid to their lord in lieu of bran which they were obliged to furnish for his hounds.

¶
'''brenningly†''', ''adv.'' Burningly; ardently. ''Chaucer.''

'''brent<sup>1</sup>''' (brent), ''a.'' [= ''brant''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.] '''1.''' Steep; upright; straight; high.—'''2.''' Smooth; unwrinkled: applied to the brow. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Your bonnie brow was ''brent.'' ''Burns,'' John Anderson.

<poem>Her fair ''brent'' brow, smooth as th’ unrunkled deep
When a’ the winds are in their caves asleep. ''Ramsay.''</poem>}}

'''brent<sup>2</sup>''' (brent), ''n.'' Same as ''brent-goose.''

'''brenta''' (bren′tä), ''n.'' [It.] An Italian liquid measure, generally equal to about 18 or 19 gallons. {{smaller|But the brenta of Crema was only 10⅕ United States gallons, and the brenta of Rome was 37.8. The last was quite exceptional.}}

'''brente''' (bren′te), ''n.'' [Cf. ''brenta.''] A Swiss liquid measure, varying in capacity from 10.31 to 17.66 gallons.

'''brent-fox''' (brent′foks), ''n.'' See ''brant-fox.''

'''brent-goose''' (brent′gös), ''n.'' [Also ''brant-goose'' and ''brand-goose'', often shortened to ''brent, brant'', G. ''brentgans'' (> prob. It. ''branta''); all due to Icel. ''brandgās'' (= Sw. ''brandgås'' = Dan. ''brandgaas''), < ''brandr'' (= Sw. Dan. ''brand'' = E. ''brand'': with reference prob. to the color; cf. ''brant-fox'') + ''gās'' = Sw. ''gås'' = Dan. ''gaas'' = E. ''goose.''] The brent or brant, a goose, ''Bernicla brenta'', of the family ''Anatidæ'', inhabiting most of the northern hemisphere. {{smaller|It is smaller than most geese, and has the head, neck, and bill black, the neck with patches of small white stripes, the tail-coverts white, and the body-colors dark. It breeds in high latitudes, migrating south}}

{{smaller block|She had her ''breeding'' at my father’s charge.
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, ii. 3.}}}}
'''4.''' Deportment or behavior in social life; manners, especially good manners: as, good ''breeding'' (politeness); a man of no ''breeding'' (that is, a very ill-bred man).
{{smaller block|<poem>As men of ''breeding'', sometimes men of wit,
T’ avoid great errors, must the less commit.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 259.}}}}
{{smaller block|In society his good ''breeding'' and vivacity made him always welcome.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Dramatists of the Restoration.}}}}
'''5†.''' Descent; extraction.
{{smaller block|Honest gentleman, I know not your ''breeding''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., v. 3.}}}}

''breósa'', ''briósa'' (only in glosses), a gadfly; not found in other tongues, and supposed to be an irreg. reduction of *''brimsa'' (also cited as AS., but not well authorized: see ''brimse'', ''brimsey'') = MD. ''bremse'', D. ''brems'' = OHG. ''brimissa'', MHG. ''brimse'', G. ''bremse'' = ODan. ''brimse'', ''bremse'', Dan. ''bremse'' = Sw. ''bremman'', roar, OHG. ''breman'', MHG. ''bremen'', roar, buzz, MHG. G. ''brummen'', D. ''brommen'', hum, buzz, grumble, L. ''fremere'', roar: see ''brim''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. Skt. ''bhramara'', a large black bee, perhaps from the same root.] A gadfly; a horse-fly; specifically, one of certain strong-bodied dipterous insects of the family ''Tabanidæ''. {{smaller|There are many species. The larvæ live in moist ground, and are subaquatic. The black breeze, ''Tabanus atratus'' (Fabricius), is one of the largest North American species. Also called ''breeze-fly''.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But he them all from him full lightly swept,
As doth a Steare, in heat of sommers day,
With his long taile the ''bryzes'' brush away.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. i. 24.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Runs like a heifer bitten with the ''brize'',
About the court. {{right|''B. Jonson'', New Inn, v. 1.}}</poem>}}

{{c|{{smaller|Black Breeze (''Tabanus atratus''). ''a'', larva; ''b'', pupa; ''c'', imago. (All slightly enlarged.)}}}}

'''breeze'''<sup>1</sup>†, ''v. i.''   [< ''breeze''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   To buzz.

'''breeze'''<sup>2</sup> (brēz), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''brize'', ''briess''; = G. ''brise'' = Dan. ''bris'', < F. ''brize'', now ''brise'', a breeze, = Sp. ''brisa'' = Pg. ''briza'', the northeast wind; cf. It. ''brezza'', a cold wind; possibly same as ''bise'', q. v., with intrusive ''-r''.]   '''1.''' A moderately brisk wind; a movement of air not so strong as a gale: as, a refreshing ''breeze''; a stiff ''breeze'' at sea.
{{smaller block|The heat of Summer [in Virginia] is in June, July and August, but commonly a cool ''Briess'' asswages the vehemency of the heat.
{{right|''S. Clarke'', Plantations of the English in America}}
{{right|[(1670), p. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|From land a gentle ''breeze'' arose at night. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''2.''' A noisy quarrel; a disturbance; a row. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|The marine went forward and gave the order; and Jemmy, who expected a ''breeze'', told his wife to behave quietly.
{{right|''Marryat'', Snarleyyow, I. xv.}}}}

'''Land-breeze, sea-breeze''', {{smaller|breezes blowing respectively from the land to or over the sea, and from the sea over the land. The former is apt to blow especially by night, and the latter by day; and in some regions this alternation occurs with great regularity. ='''Syn.''' ''Gust'', etc. See ''wind'', ''n''.}}

'''breeze'''<sup>2</sup> (brēz), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''breezed'', ppr. ''breezing''.   [< ''breeze''<sup>2</sup>, ''n''.]   To blow gently. [Rare.] —{{smaller|'''To breeze up''' (''naut.''), to blow with greater strength; freshen.}}

'''breeze'''<sup>3</sup> (brēz), ''n''.   [= E. dial. ''briss''<sup>2</sup> (q. v.), dust, rubbish, < F. ''bris'', rubbish, fragments, breakage, etc., < ''briser'', break: see ''bruise'' and ''brazil'', and cf. ''debris''. But in sense 2 perhaps < OF. ''brese'', cinders, orig. live coals, F. ''braise'', live coals: see ''braise''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' House-sweepings, as fluff, dust, ashes, etc.—'''2.''' The material sifted out from house-ashes, extensively used in burning bricks; cinders. [Eng.]

'''breeze-fly''' (brēz′flī), ''n''. Same as ''breeze''<sup>1</sup>.

'''breeze-oven''' (brēz′uv″n), ''n''. '''1.''' An oven for the manufacture of small coke.—'''2.''' A furnace designed to consume breeze or coal-dust.

'''breezy''' (brē′zi), ''a''.   [< ''breeze''<sup>2</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Of the nature of a breeze; blowy; windy.
{{smaller block|The ''breezy'' call of incense-breathing morn.
{{right|''Gray'', Elegy.}}}}
'''2.''' Fanned with gentle winds or breezes: as, the ''breezy'' shore.—'''3.''' Figuratively, brisk; lively; sprightly: as, a ''breezy'' essay.
{{smaller block|The chapter on “Value” is particularly fresh and ''breezy''.
{{right|''The American'', VIII. 87.}}}}

'''bregma''' (breg′mä̤), ''n''.; pl. ''bregmata'' (-ma̤-tä̤).   [NL., < Gr. βρέγμα, also βρέχμα, the front part of the head, sinciput, prob. < βρέχειν, wet, moisten; perhaps akin to E. ''rain'', q. v.]   In ''anat.'', the junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures of the skull; the anterior fontanel. {{smaller|It was so named because in infants it is soft, and was thought to correspond with the most humid part of the brain. Also written ''brechma'' and ''brechmus''. See cut under ''craniometry''.}}

'''Bregmaceros''' (breg-mas′e-ros), ''n.''   [NL., < Gr. βρέγμα, the front part of the head, the sinciput, + κέρας, horn.]   A genus of anacanthine fishes,
containing a few small pelagic species, and representing in some systems a family ''Bregmacerotidæ.''

[[File:century v01 p0701 c2f1.png|center|312px]]
{{c|{{smaller|''Bregmaceros atlanticus.''}}}}

'''bregmacerotid''' (breg″mạ-se-rot′id), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Bregmacerotidæ.''

'''Bregmacerotidæ''' (breg″mạ-se-rot′i-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Bregmaceros'' (''-rot-'') + ''-idæ.'']   A family of gadoid fishes, typified by the genus ''Bregmaceros.'' {{smaller|They have a robust caudal portion truncate or convex behind, almost without procurrent caudal rays above or below, with an antemedian anus, moderate suborbitals, terminal mouth, jugular ventrals abnormally developed, an occipital ray, a continuous dorsal fin mostly confined to the caudal portion, and an anal nearly similar to the long dorsal. The few known species are of small size, and inhabitants of the high or deep seas; their nearest relatives are supposed to be the codfishes.}}

'''bregmata,''' ''n.'' Plural of ''bregma.''

'''bregmatic''' (breg-mat′ik), ''a.''   [< ''bregma''(''t''-) + -''ic.'']   Of or pertaining to the bregma: as, ''bregmatic'' tension.

'''brehon''' (bre′hon), ''n.''   [< OIr. ''brithem,'' a judge, Ir. Gael. ''breitheamh,'' a judge, < OIr. ''breth,'' Ir. Gael. ''breith,'' f., OIr. Ir. ''brāth,'' m., judgment, decision.]   One of the ancient hereditary judges of Ireland, similar to those of Scotland during its Celtic period.
{{smaller block|In the territories of each sept, judges, called ''Brehons,'' and taken out of certain families, sat with primeval simplicity on turfen benches in some conspicuous situation, to determine controversies.
{{right|''Hallam,'' Const. Hist., III. 330.}}}}
{{smaller block|'''Brehon laws,''' the ancient system of laws of Ireland. These laws, originally unwritten, and developed by the brehons, were largely embodied at an early period in certain ancient writings known now as ''Brehon Tracts.'' Of these two have been translated: the ''Senchus Mor,'' or Great Book of the Law, compiled, it is said, by nine “pillars of Erin,” under the superintendence of St. Patrick; and the ''Book of Aicill,'' containing the wisdom of two of the most famous brehons, the “Royal Cormac” and the “Learned Cennfaelah.” This system of law was not entirely superseded by English laws among the native Irish until about 1650.}}

'''breithauptite''' (brīt′houp-tīt), ''n.''   [After the German mineralogist J. A. F. ''Breithaupt'' (1791–1873).]   An antimonide of nickel occurring in hexagonal crystals and also in massive forms. It has a copper-red color and brilliant metallic luster.

'''breitoline''' (brī′tō-lin), ''n.''   [Named for the inventor, L. ''Breit.'']   A musical instrument of the violin family, having five metal strings and a compass somewhat lower than a viola. It is fastened upon a table, like a zither, and played with a bow.

'''breloque''' (bre-lok′), ''n.''   [F.; origin uncertain.]   A seal, locket, charm, or other small trinket or article of jewelry attached to a watch-chain.

'''breme†''', ''a.'' See ''brim''<sup>4</sup>.

'''bremely†''', ''adv.'' See ''brimly.''

'''Bremen blue, green,''' etc. See the nouns.

'''bremly†''', ''adv.'' See ''brimly.''

'''bren<sup>1</sup>†''' (bren), ''v.''   [< ME. ''brennen'', the usual form of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   An obsolete or dialectal variant of ''burn''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Closely the wicked flame his bowels ''brent.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. vii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Romaines this Night [Candlemas Day] went about the City of Rome, with Torches and Candles ''brenning'' in Worship of this Woman Februa, for hope to have the more Helpe and Succoure of her sonne Mars.
{{right|''J. Brand'', in Bourne’s Pop. Antiq. (1777), p. 224.}}}}

'''bren<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' An obsolete variant of ''bran''<sup>1</sup>. ''Chaucer.''

'''brennage''' (bren′āj), ''n.''   [< OF. ''brenage'' (ML. ''brenagium''), < ''bren'', ML. ''brennium'', bran: see ''bran''<sup>1</sup>.]   In ''old law'', a tribute or composition which tenants paid to their lord in lieu of bran which they were obliged to furnish for his hounds.

'''brenningly†''', ''adv.'' Burningly; ardently. ''Chaucer.''

'''brent<sup>1</sup>''' (brent), ''a.''   [= ''brant''<sup>1</sup>, q. v.]   '''1.''' Steep; upright; straight; high.—'''2.''' Smooth; unwrinkled: applied to the brow. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Your bonnie brow was ''brent.'' ''Burns,'' John Anderson.

<poem>Her fair ''brent'' brow, smooth as th’ unrunkled deep
When a’ the winds are in their caves asleep. ''Ramsay.''</poem>}}

'''brent<sup>2</sup>''' (brent), ''n.'' Same as ''brent-goose.''

'''brenta''' (bren′tä), ''n.''   [It.]   An Italian liquid measure, generally equal to about 18 or 19 gallons. {{smaller|But the brenta of Crema was only 10⅕ United States gallons, and the brenta of Rome was 37.8. The last was quite exceptional.}}

'''brente''' (bren′te), ''n.''   [Cf. ''brenta.'']   A Swiss liquid measure, varying in capacity from 10.31 to 17.66 gallons.

'''brent-fox''' (brent′foks), ''n.'' See ''brant-fox.''

'''brent-goose''' (brent′gös), ''n.''   [Also ''brant-goose'' and ''brand-goose'', often shortened to ''brent, brant'', G. ''brentgans'' (> prob. It. ''branta''); all due to Icel. ''brandgās'' (= Sw. ''brandgås'' = Dan. ''brandgaas''), < ''brandr'' (= Sw. Dan. ''brand'' = E. ''brand'': with reference prob. to the color; cf. ''brant-fox'') + ''gās'' = Sw. ''gås'' = Dan. ''gaas'' = E. ''goose.'']   The brent or brant, a goose, ''Bernicla brenta'', of the family ''Anatidæ'', inhabiting most of the northern hemisphere. {{smaller|It is smaller than most geese, and has the head, neck, and bill black, the neck with patches of small white stripes, the tail-coverts white, and the body-colors dark. It breeds in high latitudes, migrating south}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
